claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1K.

claims.claim: Slc6a17 was also expressed in the basolateral amygdala (BLA).
claims.source: Slc6a17 was also expressed in the basolateral amygdala (BLA) (Figure 1J), a brain area essential for emotion and fear learning.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 1J.

claims.claim: Slc6a17-KO mice were not significantly different from the wild type (WT, Slc6a17+/+) mice in body weight.
claims.source: These Slc6a17-KO mice were not significantly different from the wild type (WT, Slc6a17+/+) mice in body weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Slc6a17-KO mice were not significantly different from the wild type mice in basal activities.
claims.source: These Slc6a17-KO mice were not significantly different from the wild type (WT, Slc6a17+/+) mice in body weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), basal activities (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Slc6a17-KO mice were not significantly different from the wild type mice in short-term memory.
claims.source: These Slc6a17-KO mice were not significantly different from the wild type (WT, Slc6a17+/+) mice in body weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), basal activities (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), or short-term memory (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Slc6a17-/- mice exhibited a significant decrease in freezing behavior in both cued and contextual fear conditioning.
claims.source: Slc6a17-/- mice exhibited a significant decrease in freezing behavior in both cued and contextual fear conditioning (day 2 context a, p=0.0062 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17-/-, p<0.0001 for Slc6a17+/- vs. Slc6a17-/-; Day 3 tone, p=0.0093 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17-/-, p=0.0012 for Slc6a17+/- vs. Slc6a17-/-).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2C with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Slc6a17-/- mice differed significantly from Slc6a17+/+ and Slc6a17+/- mice in latency to find the hidden platform during the training session of Morris water maze.
claims.source: Slc6a17-/- mice differed significantly from Slc6a17+/+ and Slc6a17+/- mice (two-way ANOVA; main effect of training day: F (4.681, 210.7) = 46.55, p<0.0001; main effect of genotype: F (2, 45) = 21.53, p<0.0001; main effect of training day × genotype: F (12, 270) = 3.762, p<0.0001; Tukey's multiple comparisons test: day 2, p=0.0004 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17-/-, p=0.0002 for Slc6a17+/- vs. Slc6a17-/-; day 5, p=0.0002 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17-/-, p=0.008 for Slc6a17+/- vs. Slc6a17-/-; day 6, p=0.0002 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17-/-, p=0.0027 for Slc6a17+/- vs. Slc6a17-/-; day 7, p<0.0001 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17-/-, p=0.0005 for Slc6a17+/- vs. Slc6a17-/-).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2E with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Percentage of time spent in the target quadrant was significantly different between Slc6a17-/- mice and control mice in Morris water maze probe trial.
claims.source: Percentage of time spent in the target quadrant was significantly different (p=0.0004 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17-/-, p<0.0001 for Slc6a17+/- vs. Slc6a17-/-).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2G with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Number of crossings through the platform area was significantly different between Slc6a17-/- mice and control mice in Morris water maze probe trial.
claims.source: Number of crossings through the platform area was significantly different (p=0.0194 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17-/-, p=0.0054 for Slc6a17+/- vs. Slc6a17-/-).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2H with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Slc6a17-KO mice are significantly impaired both in contextual and cued fear memory and in hippocampus-dependent spatial learning and memory.
claims.source: Taken together, these data indicate that Slc6a17-KO mice are significantly impaired both in contextual and cued fear memory and in hippocampus-dependent spatial learning and memory.
claims.evidence: This statement is a summary of the behavioral data presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Slc6a17P633R/P633R mutant mice were not significantly different from the WT or heterozygous in body weight.
claims.source: Homozygous (Slc6a17P633R/P633R) mutant mice were not significantly different from the WT (Slc6a17+/+) or heterozygous (Slc6a17P633R/+) in body weight (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Slc6a17P633R/P633R mutant mice were not significantly different from the WT or heterozygous in basal activities.
claims.source: Homozygous (Slc6a17P633R/P633R) mutant mice were not significantly different from the WT (Slc6a17+/+) or heterozygous (Slc6a17P633R/+) in body weight (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), basal activities (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Slc6a17P633R/P633R mutant mice were not significantly different from the WT or heterozygous in novel objection recognition.
claims.source: Homozygous (Slc6a17P633R/P633R) mutant mice were not significantly different from the WT (Slc6a17+/+) or heterozygous (Slc6a17P633R/+) in body weight (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), basal activities (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), or novel objection recognition (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: Slc6a17P633R homozygous mutants exhibited significant decrease of freezing behavior in both cued and contextual fear conditioning.
claims.source: Slc6a17P633R homozygous mutants exhibited significant decrease of freezing behavior in both cued and contextual fear conditioning (day 2 context A, p<0.0001 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R, p<0.0001 for Slc6a17P633R/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R; Day 3 tone, p=0.0017 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R, p=0.0009 for Slc6a17P633R/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3D with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Slc6a17P633R/P633R mice showed significantly different learning curve from Slc6a17+/+ and Slc6a17P633R/+ mice in Morris water maze.
claims.source: Slc6a17P633R/P633R mice showed significantly different learning curve from Slc6a17+/+ and Slc6a17P633R/+ mice (two-way ANOVA; main effect of training day: F (4.381, 144.6) = 20.02, p<0.0001; main effect of genotype: F (2, 33) = 22.65, p<0.0001; main effect of training day × genotype: F (12, 198) = 2.389, p=0.0067; Tukey's multiple-comparisons test: day 2, p=0.0150 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R, p=0.0078 for Slc6a17P633R/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R; day 3, p=0.0403 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R, p=0.0388 for Slc6a17P633R/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R; day 5, p=0.0023 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R, p=0.0243 for Slc6a17P633R/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R; day 6, p=0.0199 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/+,p=0.0010 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R, p=0.0077 for Slc6a17P633R/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R; day 7, p=0.0074 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R, p=0.0129 for Slc6a17P633R/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3F with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Percentage of time spent in the target quadrant was significantly different between Slc6a17P633R/P633R mice and control mice in Morris water maze probe trial.
claims.source: Percentage of time spent in the target quadrant was significantly different (p=0.0031 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R, p=0.0325 for Slc6a17P633R/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3H with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Number of crossings through the platform area was significantly different between Slc6a17P633R/P633R mice and control mice in Morris water maze probe trial.
claims.source: Number of crossings through the platform area was significantly different (p=0.0003 for Slc6a17+/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R, p=0.0123 for Slc6a17P633R/+ vs. Slc6a17P633R/P633R).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3I with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Slc6a17P633R mice are significantly impaired both in contextual and cued fear memory and in hippocampus-dependent long-term spatial learning.
claims.source: Taken together, these data indicate that Slc6a17P633R mice are also significantly impaired both in contextual and cued fear memory and in hippocampus-dependent long-term spatial learning.
claims.evidence: This statement is a summary of the behavioral data presented in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The point mutation P633R is a LOF mutation.
claims.source: Because all the phenotypes of Slc6a17P633R are similar to Slc6a7-KO, the point mutation P633R is a LOF mutation.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on the similarity of phenotypes between Slc6a17P633R and Slc6a17-KO mice.

claims.claim: SLC6A17-HA was enriched in LP2 fraction, similar to other SV proteins.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, SLC6A17-HA was enriched in LP2 fraction, similar to the other SV proteins such as synaptotagmin 1 (Syt1) (Geppert et al., 1994), vesicular ATPase (V-ATPase) (Cidon and Sihra, 1989), and synaptobrevin 2 (Syb2) (Link et al., 1992; Schiavo et al., 1992), but different from postsynaptic proteins such as postsynaptic density 95 (PSD95) (Cho et al., 1992; Woods and Bryant, 1991).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and citations to published literature.

claims.claim: Sucrose gradient centrifugation of the LP2 fraction showed copurification of SLC6A17-HA with SV proteins.
claims.source: Sucrose gradient centrifugation of the LP2 fraction showed copurification of SLC6A17-HA with SV proteins including synaptophysin (Syp) (Jahn et al., 1985; Leube et al., 1987; Wiedenmann and Franke, 1985), Syt1, and VGluT1 (Bellocchio et al., 2000; Takamori et al., 2000), but not with proteins localized to the postsynaptic membrane (PSD95) or (SNAP23) (Ravichandran et al., 1996; Suh et al., 2010), the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (ERp72), the endosome (EEA1) (Mu et al., 1995), and the proteosome (PSMC6) or the trans-Golgi network (synaptaxin 6, STX6) (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and citations to published literature.

claims.claim: The fraction containing SLC6A17-HA was found to be co-localized with SV markers.
claims.source: After examining markers of subcellular organelles, the fraction containing SLC6A17-HA was found to be co-localized with SV markers such as Syp, Syt1, Syb2, VATPase, and vesicular neurotransmitter transporters including VGluT1, VGluT2, and VGAT (Figure 4C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The fraction containing SLC6A17-HA was not co-localized with markers of various non-SV organelles.
claims.source: but not with markers of axons or dendrites (GLUT4 or transferrin receptor), ER (ERp72), the lysosome (LAMP2, LC3b, or cathepsin D), the cytoplasmic membrane (SNAP23, PSD95, and GluN1), the Golgi apparatus (GM130 and Goglin-97), mitochondria (VADC), the active zone (ERC1b/2), the endosome (EEA1), and the proteosome (PSMC6) (Figure 4C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Immunostaining of HA-tagged SLC6A17 in Slc6a17HA/+ mouse showed puncta co-localized with the anti-Syp positive immunoreactivity.
claims.source: In addition, immunostaining of HA-tagged SLC6A17 in Slc6a17HA/+ mouse showed puncta co-localized with the anti-Syp positive immunoreactivity (Figure 4B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and B).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: SLC6A17-APEX2 was indeed localized on the SVs.
claims.source: SLC6A17-APEX2 was indeed localized on the SVs (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, C, E, and G).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Quantitative analysis showed distinct populations of SVs distinguished by electron density.
claims.source: Quantitative analysis showed distinct populations of SVs distinguished by electron density (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, D, F, and H).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: SLC6A17 was the only transporter significantly decreased in Slc6a17-KO mice.
claims.source: Quantitative proteomic analysis showed that only SLC6A17 was dramatically reduced in SVs immunopurified from Slc6a17-KO mice, whereas other transporters such as VGluT1, VGluT2, VGluT3, VGAT, VMAT2, SV2A, SV2B, SV2C, ZnT3, and VAT-1 were not different between Slc6a17-/- and Slc6a17+/+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: SLC6A17P633R-HA signal was primarily localized to the soma with no overlap detected with the anti-Syp antibody staining.
claims.source: With the endogenous SLC6A17P633R protein tagged by the HA and FLAG epitopes (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), we found that SLC6A17P633R-HA signal was primarily localized to the soma with no overlap detected with the anti-Syp antibody staining (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: HA and FLAG signals were presented in LP2 but did not co-purified with SVs in sucrose gradients, indicated that the SLC6A17P633R protein was not present in SVs.
claims.source: We also performed differential centrifugation and sucrose gradient purification. HA and FLAG signals were presented in LP2 but did not co-purified with SVs in sucrose gradients, indicated that the SLC6A17P633R protein was not present in SVs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Glu, GABA, and ACh were reliably detected from SVs immunoisolated with the anti-Syp antibody.
claims.source: Glu, GABA, and ACh were reliably detected from SVs immunoisolated with the anti-Syp antibody (Figure 5C–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, D, and F).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Of the nine AAs reported previously using cultured cells, eight (Ala, Gly, Leu, Pro, Cys, Gly, His, and Ser) were not found to be significantly enriched in SVs.
claims.source: Surprisingly, of the nine AAs reported previously using cultured cells, eight (Ala, Gly, Leu, Pro, Cys, Gly, His, and Ser) were not found to be significantly enriched in SVs (Figure 5C and D).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claims.claim: Only Gln was reproducibly found to be enriched in the anti-Syp antibody immunoisolated SVs.
claims.source: Only Gln was reproducibly found to be enriched in the anti-Syp antibody immunoisolated SVs (Figure 5C, D and H).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 5C, D, and H.

claims.claim: Significant enrichment of Gln was detected in SVs containing SLC6A17-HA.
claims.source: Significant enrichment of Gln was detected in SVs containing SLC6A17-HA (Figure 6C, D, and H).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6C, D, and H.

claims.claim: The other eight AAs had not been found to be enriched in SVs containing SLC6A17-HA.
claims.source: By contrast, the other eight AAs had not been found to be enriched in SVs containing SLC6A17-HA (Figure 6C, D, and I).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 6C, D, and I.

claims.claim: The overexpressed SLC6A17-HA protein was localized in SVs.
claims.source: The overexpressed SLC6A17-HA protein was localized in SVs, as analyzed by immunoblot (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: SVs from mice overexpressing SLC6A17-HA contained significantly higher levels of Glu and GABA.
claims.source: SVs from mice overexpressing SLC6A17-HA contained significantly higher levels of Glu and GABA (Figure 7B–G).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7B-G.

claims.claim: Gln was dramatically increased in SVs overexpressing SLC6A17-HA.
claims.source: Gln was dramatically increased (Figure 7B and F), to the extent that Gln was higher than GABA in SVs overexpressing SLC6A17-HA (Figure 7B, D, F, K, and M).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7B, F, K, and M.

claims.claim: Quantification of the enriched molecules in SVs containing SLC6A17-HA showed Gln to be approximately two times that of GABA.
claims.source: Quantification of the enriched molecules in SVs containing SLC6A17-HA showed Gln to be approximately two times that of GABA (Figure 7D and F).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7D and F.

claims.claim: His was moderately increased in SVs overexpressing SLC6A17-HA.
claims.source: In addition, His was moderately increased in SVs overexpressing SLC6A17-HA (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, D).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, D.

claims.claim: Overexpressed SLC6A17G162R-HA was still localized on SVs.
claims.source: Overexpressed SLC6A17G162R-HA was still localized on SVs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, E).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and E.

claims.claim: Levels of Glu and GABA in SVs containing SLC6A17G162R-HA were higher than those in WT mice.
claims.source: Levels of Glu and GABA in SVs containing SLC6A17G162R-HA were higher than those in WT mice (Figure 7J and K, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), but not significantly different with those from OE-Syp-HA mice (Figure 7J and K).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7J, K, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The level of Gln in SVs containing SLC6A17G162R-HA were much lower than that in from OE-SLC6A17-HA mice.
claims.source: The level of Gln in SVs containing SLC6A17G162R-HA were much lower than that in from OE-SLC6A17-HA mice (Figure 7M), indicating that SLC6A17G162R was defective in transporting Gln into SVs in vivo.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7M.

claims.claim: SLC6A17G162R was defective in transporting Gln into SVs in vivo.
claims.source: The level of Gln in SVs containing SLC6A17G162R-HA were much lower than that in from OE-SLC6A17-HA mice (Figure 7M), indicating that SLC6A17G162R was defective in transporting Gln into SVs in vivo.
claims.evidence: This statement is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 7M.

claims.claim: The level of Gln in SVs containing SLC6A17G162R-HA was higher than that in WT mice, but not different from that in OE-Syp-HA mice.
claims.source: The level of Gln in SVs containing SLC6A17G162R-HA was higher than that in WT mice, but not different from that in OE-Syp-HA mice (Figure 7M).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7M.

claims.claim: Gln was increased most dramatically in SVs overexpressing SLC6A17-HA, compared to those overexpressing Syp-HA or SLC6A17G162R-HA.
claims.source: Gln was increased most dramatically in SVs overexpressing SLC6A17-HA, compared to those overexpressing Syp-HA (Figure 7I and M) or SLC6A17G162R-HA (Figure 7H and M).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7H, I, and M.

claims.claim: Gln was the only molecule found to be decreased in SVs from Slc6a17-/- mice, compared with Slc6a17+/+ or Slc6a17+/- mice.
claims.source: LC-MS analysis of SVs revealed that Gln was the only molecule found to be decreased in SVs from Slc6a17-/- mice, compared with Slc6a17+/+ or Slc6a17+/- mice (Figure 8H).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 8H.

claims.claim: The levels of classic transmitters such as Glu, GABA, and ACh were not significantly different among the SVs immunoisolated from the Slc6a17+/+, the Slc6a17+/-, or the Slc6a17-/- mice.
claims.source: Quantitative analysis showed that the levels of classic transmitters such as Glu (Figure 8A), GABA (Figure 8B), and ACh (Figure 8C) were not significantly different among the SVs immunoisolated from the Slc6a17+/+, the Slc6a17+/-, or the Slc6a17-/- mice.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 8A, B, and C.

claims.claim: The levels of the other eight AAs were also not significantly different among SVs immunoisolated from all three genotypes.
claims.source: The levels of the other eight AAs were also not significantly different among SVs immunoisolated from all three genotypes (Figure 8D–F, G, I– L).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 8D-L.

claims.claim: Slc6a17-HA was significantly reduced both in the homogenates of total brains and in immunoisolated SVs from AAV-sgRNA/Slc6a17iCre/Cas9+ mice.
claims.source: Slc6a17-HA was significantly reduced both in the homogenates of total brains and in immunoisolated SVs from AAV-sgRNA/Slc6a17iCre/Cas9+ mice (Figure 9B, Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Gln was the only vesicular content significantly decreased in SVs from the knockout mice.
claims.source: Importantly, when the SV contents from the brains of knockout (AAV-sgRNA/Slc6a17iCre/Cas9+) and control (AAV-sgRNA/Slc6a17iCre/Cas9-) mice were compared after LC-MS analysis, Gln was the only vesicular content significantly decreased in SVs from the knockout mice (Figure 9C, D, and H).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 9C, D, and H.

claims.claim: GABA and Glu were moderately increased in SVs from adult Slc6a17 knockout mice.
claims.source: To our surprise, GABA and Glu were moderately increased (Figure 9C–F).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 9C-F.

claims.claim: The level of ACh, and those of the other eight AAs (Ala, Gly, Leu, Pro, Cys, Gly, His, and Ser), was not significantly changed in the SVs from adult Slc6a17 knockout mice.
claims.source: The level of ACh, and those of the other eight AAs (Ala, Gly, Leu, Pro, Cys, Gly, His, and Ser), was not significantly changed in the SVs from adult Slc6a17 knockout mice (Figure 9C, D, G, and I).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 9C, D, G, and I.

claims.claim: SLC6A17 is physiologically necessary for Gln in SVs, but not for the other eight AAs.
claims.source: These results indicate that SLC6A17 is physiologically necessary for Gln in SVs, but not for the other eight AAs.
claims.evidence: This statement is a summary of the data from the virally mediated knockout experiment.

claims.claim: Gln transport into the SVs was decreased in Slc6a17P633R mutant mice.
claims.source: Gln transport into the SVs was decreased in Slc6a17P633R mutant mice (Figure 10I).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 10H.

claims.claim: A significant decrease in Gln level in Slc6a17P633R/P633R, compared to Slc6a17+/+ and Slc6a17P633R/+ mice.
claims.source: LC-MS analysis of contents from SVs showed a significant decrease in Gln level in Slc6a17P633R/P633R, compared to Slc6a17+/+ and Slc6a17P633R/+ mice (Figure 10H).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 10H.

claims.claim: The levels of Glu, GABA, and ACh in SVs were not significantly different among Slc6a17+/+, Slc6a17P633R/+, and Slc6a17P633R/P633R mice.
claims.source: The levels of Glu (Figure 10A), GABA (Figure 10B), and ACh (Figure 10C) in SVs were not significantly different among Slc6a17+/+, Slc6a17P633R/+, and Slc6a17P633R/P633R mice.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 10A, B, and C.

claims.claim: The levels of the other eight AAs in the SVs were also not significantly different among Slc6a17+/+, Slc6a17P633R/+, and Slc6a17P633R/P633R mice.
claims.source: The levels of the other eight AAs in the SVs were also not significantly different among Slc6a17+/+, Slc6a17P633R/+, and Slc6a17P633R/P633R mice (Figure 10D–G, I–L).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 10D-L.

claims.claim: Mislocalization of SLC6A17P633R outside the SVs correlates with the inability of Gln enrichment in SVs.
claims.source: Thus, mislocalization of SLC6A17P633R outside the SVs correlates with the inability of Gln enrichment in SVs (Figure 10H), as well as behavioral impairment (Figure 3D, F, H, and I), establishing the significance of SLC6A17 localization on the SVs.
claims.evidence: This statement is an inference based on the correlation between mislocalization and Gln reduction.

claims.claim: Two mutations pathogenic for human ID both resulted in reduction of Gln in the SVs.
claims.source: We have discovered the presence of Gln in the SVs and shown that it is functionally important because two mutations pathogenic for human ID patients both resulted in reduction of Gln in the SVs.
claims.evidence: This statement is a summary of the findings from the two point mutation studies.

claims.claim: The human ID mutation Slc6a17P633R causes mislocalization of SLC6A17 outside the SVs.
claims.source: We demonstrate the functional significance of the SV localization of SLC6A17 by showing that the human ID mutation Slc6a17P633R causes mislocalization of SLC6A17 outside the SVs (Figure 3B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: SLC6A17 is sufficient for Gln presence in SVs.
claims.source: With multiple rounds of biochemical purification of SVs and chemical analysis of SV contents of genetically modified mice, we have found that Gln is present in SVs containing SLC6A17 and that SLC6A17 is sufficient for Gln presence in SVs (Figures 5—7).
claims.evidence: This statement is a summary of the findings from the overexpression experiments.

claims.claim: Gln is the only molecule reliably and reproducibly reduced in SVs when Slc6a17 gene is deleted.
claims.source: With two lines of germline mutant mice and virally mediated gene edited mice, we demonstrate that Gln is the only molecule reliably and reproducibly reduced in SVs when Slc6a17 gene is deleted (Figures 8 and 9).
claims.evidence: This statement is a summary of the findings from the knockout experiments.

claims.claim: SLC6A17G162R could not transport Gln into SVs.
claims.source: We have also characterized mice carrying a human ID mutation SLC6A17G162R and found it could not transport Gln into SVs (Figure 7), further supporting the importance of Gln in SVs.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Two mutations pathogenic in human ID are both LOF mutations: SLC6A17P633R with mislocalization outside the SVs and the SLC6A17G162R with defective Gln transport into the SVs.
claims.source: Thus, two mutations pathogenic in human ID are both LOF mutations: SLC6A17P633R with mislocalization outside the SVs and the SLC6A17G162R with defective Gln transport into the SVs.
claims.evidence: This statement is a summary of the findings from the two point mutation studies.

claims.claim: All four kinds of SLC6A17 LOF mutations (two KOs, two point mutations) have led to reduction in Gln in SVs.
claims.source: The fact that all four kinds of SLC6A17 LOF mutations (two KOs, two point mutations) have led to reduction in Gln in SVs strongly support the functional significance of Gln in SVs.
claims.evidence: This statement is a summary of the findings from all the genetic manipulation experiments.

claims.claim: SLC6A17 is a member of the SLC6 family, which is also known as the NTT family because many members of this family are transporters for neurotransmitters.
claims.source: SLC6A17 is a member of the SLC6 family, which is also known as the NTT family because many members of this family are transporters for neurotransmitters (Blakely and Edwards, 2012; Bröer, 2006; Kristensen et al., 2011; Rudnick et al., 2014)
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: There is a Glu/Gln cycle in which Glu released from neurons is taken up by glia and transformed into Gln, followed by Gln release from glia and taken up by neurons and transformed into Glu.
claims.source: There is a Glu/Gln cycle in which Glu released from neurons is taken up by glia and transformed into Gln, followed by Gln release from glia and taken up by neurons and transformed into Glu (Bak et al., 2006; Benjamin and Quastel, 1972; Ottersen et al., 1992; van den Berg and Garfinkel, 1971).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claims.claim: It is unlikely that SLC6A17 and the Gln transports could be part of the Glu/Gln cycle.
claims.source: It is unlikely that SLC6A17 and the Gln transports could be part of the Glu/Gln cycle because (1) the Glu/Gln cycle uses cytoplasmic transporters for Gln, not vesicular transporters for Gln; (2) Gln is transformed into Glu in the cytoplasm of neurons before being transported in the SVs as Glu; and (3) in all of our experiments presented here, when SLC6A17 was genetically disrupted, Gln was consistently decreased, but Glu was either unchanged but not concomitantly increased, which was against the expectation of the Glu/Gln cycle.
claims.evidence: This statement is based on logical inference from the data and knowledge of the Glu/Gln cycle.

claims.claim: Gln is one of the major carbon sources.
claims.source: The possibility of Gln as a carbon source is based on the fact that it is one of the major carbon sources (Hensley et al., 2013; Reitzer et al., 1979).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

results.result: Slc6a17 expression pattern was mapped in the mouse brain using a Slc6a17-2A-CreERT2 knock-in mouse crossed with Ai14 reporter mice. Strong expression was detected in the dentate gyrus and CA3 region of the hippocampus, with little expression in CA1 or CA2, and expression was also found in the basolateral amygdala, neocortex, thalamus, pontine nuclei, and brainstem.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 are supported by immunofluorescence data from the Slc6a17-2A-CreERT2::Ai14 reporter mice shown in Figure 1. The expression pattern is clearly documented with anatomical specificity, showing regional distribution across multiple brain areas with particular detail in hippocampal subregions.

results.result: Slc6a17 knockout mice exhibit significant deficits in learning and memory. While Slc6a17-/- mice showed no differences from wild-type in body weight, basal activity, or short-term memory, they displayed significant impairments in both contextual and cued fear conditioning, as well as in hippocampus-dependent spatial learning and memory in the Morris water maze.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C29 are well-supported by comprehensive behavioral data with appropriate statistical analyses (Figures 2 and supplements). The fear conditioning and Morris water maze experiments include proper controls (WT and heterozygous mice), adequate sample sizes (n=15-23), and show consistent deficits across multiple memory tasks with significant p-values reported.

results.result: Slc6a17P633R point mutant mice, modeling a human ID mutation, phenocopy the Slc6a17 knockout mice. Homozygous Slc6a17P633R/P633R mice showed no differences in body weight, basal activity, or novel object recognition, but exhibited significant impairments in both fear conditioning and Morris water maze performance similar to knockout mice, indicating that P633R is a loss-of-function mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C38 are supported by behavioral data from the Slc6a17P633R mice (Figure 3) with appropriate statistical analyses and sample sizes (n=9-18). The phenotypic similarity to knockout mice provides strong evidence that P633R is a LOF mutation, though this conclusion relies on phenotypic comparison rather than direct functional assessment.

results.result: SLC6A17 protein is localized to synaptic vesicles. Multiple approaches including differential centrifugation, sucrose gradient purification, immunoisolation with anti-HA antibodies from Slc6a17-HA knock-in mice, immunofluorescence, and APEX2-based electron microscopy all demonstrate that SLC6A17 co-localizes with synaptic vesicle markers and is present on synaptic vesicles.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C45 are strongly supported by convergent evidence from multiple independent techniques (Figure 4 and supplements). The biochemical fractionation shows co-purification with SV markers, immunofluorescence shows co-localization with synaptophysin, and EM with APEX2 provides direct visualization of SLC6A17 on SVs. The use of multiple orthogonal methods strengthens confidence in this localization.

results.result: Quantitative proteomic analysis of synaptic vesicles from Slc6a17-KO mice showed that SLC6A17 was the only transporter significantly decreased, while other vesicular transporters (VGluT1, VGluT2, VGluT3, VGAT, VMAT2, SV2A, SV2B, SV2C, ZnT3, VAT-1) were unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claim C46 is supported by TMT-labeled quantitative proteomics data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The volcano plot clearly shows SLC6A17 as the only significantly reduced transporter, validating the specificity of the knockout and ruling out compensatory changes in other vesicular transporters.

results.result: The SLC6A17P633R mutant protein is mislocalized outside of synaptic vesicles. Immunostaining showed SLC6A17P633R-HA signal primarily in the soma with no overlap with synaptophysin, and biochemical fractionation showed that while the mutant protein was present in LP2, it did not co-purify with SVs in sucrose gradients.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 are supported by immunofluorescence (Figure 3B) and biochemical fractionation data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). The convergent evidence from imaging and biochemistry demonstrates mislocalization of the P633R mutant, providing a mechanistic explanation for the behavioral phenotype.

results.result: LC-MS analysis of synaptic vesicles immunoisolated with anti-synaptophysin antibody revealed that glutamine (Gln) was the only amino acid among nine previously reported SLC6A17 substrates that was significantly enriched in SVs. Classical neurotransmitters (Glu, GABA, ACh) were reliably detected, but eight other amino acids (Ala, Gly, Leu, Pro, Cys, His, Ser) were not significantly enriched.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 are supported by LC-MS data with appropriate controls (anti-Syp vs IgG) and statistical analysis (Figure 5). The volcano plot and quantification clearly show Gln enrichment while other previously reported substrates are not enriched. However, the manuscript notes that relative abundance and detectability may vary, so absence of detection doesn't definitively rule out transport of other substrates.

results.result: Glutamine was significantly enriched in synaptic vesicles containing SLC6A17-HA immunoisolated from Slc6a17-HA knock-in mice, while the other eight previously reported amino acid substrates were not enriched.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 are supported by LC-MS analysis of SVs immunoisolated with anti-HA beads from Slc6a17HA/+ mice compared to WT controls (Figure 6). This provides independent confirmation of Gln enrichment in SLC6A17-containing vesicles using a different purification strategy than the anti-Syp approach.

results.result: Viral overexpression of SLC6A17-HA in mouse brain dramatically increased glutamine levels in synaptic vesicles. SVs from mice overexpressing SLC6A17-HA contained significantly higher levels of Glu and GABA, but Gln was increased most dramatically—to approximately twice the level of GABA. Histidine was moderately increased.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 are supported by LC-MS analysis of SVs from AAV-mediated SLC6A17-HA overexpression (Figure 7). The data demonstrate sufficiency of SLC6A17 for Gln transport. However, the increases in Glu and GABA may reflect general SV enrichment rather than direct transport by SLC6A17, and the His increase requires further validation as noted by the authors.

results.result: The SLC6A17G162R mutant protein, modeling another human ID mutation, was still localized on SVs but was defective in glutamine transport. While Glu and GABA levels in SVs containing SLC6A17G162R-HA were higher than WT, they were not different from Syp-HA overexpression controls. Gln levels in SLC6A17G162R-containing SVs were much lower than in SLC6A17-HA overexpressing mice and not different from Syp-HA controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 are supported by localization data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and LC-MS analysis comparing SLC6A17-HA, SLC6A17G162R-HA, and Syp-HA overexpression (Figure 7). The comparison with Syp-HA control is critical for distinguishing specific Gln transport from general SV enrichment, and the data clearly show G162R is defective specifically for Gln transport while maintaining SV localization.

results.result: In Slc6a17 knockout mice, glutamine was the only molecule significantly decreased in synaptic vesicles compared to wild-type and heterozygous mice. Classical neurotransmitters (Glu, GABA, ACh) and the other eight amino acids showed no significant differences among genotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 are supported by LC-MS analysis of SVs from Slc6a17+/+, +/-, and -/- mice (Figure 8). The data demonstrate necessity of SLC6A17 for Gln in SVs. Sample sizes are adequate (n=12 per group) and statistical analyses are appropriate. This is a critical loss-of-function experiment establishing SLC6A17's role in Gln transport.

results.result: Virally mediated CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of Slc6a17 in adult mice confirmed that SLC6A17 is physiologically necessary for Gln in SVs. Gln was the only vesicular content significantly decreased in knockout mice, while ACh and the other eight amino acids were unchanged. Surprisingly, GABA and Glu were moderately increased.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 are partially supported by the viral knockout experiment (Figure 9). While Gln decrease is clearly demonstrated, the unexpected increases in Glu and GABA (C70) are inconsistent with the germline knockout results (C66) where these neurotransmitters were unchanged. The authors acknowledge this discrepancy but don't provide a clear explanation. This inconsistency raises questions about the interpretation, though the Gln-specific effect remains robust.

results.result: In Slc6a17P633R mutant mice, glutamine levels in synaptic vesicles were significantly decreased compared to wild-type and heterozygous mice, while levels of Glu, GABA, ACh, and the other eight amino acids were not significantly different. This demonstrates that mislocalization of SLC6A17P633R outside SVs correlates with inability to enrich Gln in SVs.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C77 are supported by LC-MS analysis of SVs from Slc6a17P633R mice (Figure 10). The data link the mislocalization phenotype (C47-C48) to functional consequences (reduced Gln in SVs), providing a mechanistic explanation for the behavioral deficits. The correlation between mislocalization and Gln reduction is strong, though C77's claim of causation is inferential.

results.result: The study establishes that both human ID mutations in SLC6A17 are loss-of-function mutations that reduce Gln in synaptic vesicles through different mechanisms: P633R causes mislocalization outside SVs, while G162R causes defective Gln transport despite proper SV localization. Multiple lines of evidence from seven types of genetically modified mice demonstrate that SLC6A17 is both necessary and sufficient for Gln presence in SVs, and that Gln is a novel molecule in SVs.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C84 represent the major conclusions synthesizing results from multiple experiments. The evidence is strong: two knockout models (germline and viral), two point mutation models, and overexpression experiments all converge on Gln as the endogenous substrate. The mechanistic distinction between the two ID mutations is well-supported. However, the claim that Gln reduction is 'the key pathogenetic mechanism' (C8) remains inferential—while the correlation is strong, direct causation hasn't been demonstrated.

results.result: Human mutations in SLC6A17 have been reported to cause intellectual disability in prior studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C10 are supported by citations to published literature (Iqbal et al., 2015; Waltl, 2015). These are background claims establishing the clinical relevance of studying SLC6A17.

results.result: Prior literature established that SLC6A17 was discovered 30 years ago, is predominantly expressed in the nervous system, and was localized to synaptic vesicles. Early efforts failed to identify substrates, but later cell culture studies reported that SLC6A17 could transport 4-9 amino acids, though none of these had been found in SVs.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C17 are background claims supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These establish the knowledge gap that the current study addresses: while SLC6A17 was known to be on SVs and could transport amino acids in cell culture, its endogenous substrate in vivo was unknown.

results.result: The authors discuss potential functions of vesicular Gln, noting that SLC6A17 belongs to the neurotransmitter transporter family, that a Glu/Gln cycle exists between neurons and glia, and that Gln is a major carbon source. They argue that vesicular Gln transport by SLC6A17 is unlikely to be part of the Glu/Gln cycle based on the use of vesicular vs. cytoplasmic transporters and the lack of concomitant Glu increases when SLC6A17 is disrupted.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 are discussion points supported by citations and logical reasoning based on the experimental data. The argument against Gln/Glu cycle involvement (C87) is reasonable given the data, though not definitive. The authors appropriately acknowledge that the actual function of vesicular Gln remains to be determined.

results.result: SLC6A17 mutations cause intellectual disability in humans, and mouse models with SLC6A17 knockout or point mutations (Slc6a17-/- and Slc6a17P633R/P633R) exhibit significant impairments in fear conditioning and spatial learning/memory tasks.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that 'the reported evidence that disease-linked SLC6A17 variants cause behavioral abnormalities is convincing.' The behavioral phenotypes in knockout and mutant mice are accepted as robust findings demonstrating the link between SLC6A17 loss-of-function and cognitive impairment.

results.result: SLC6A17 protein is localized on synaptic vesicles, as demonstrated by biochemical fractionation, immunostaining, proteomic analysis, and electron microscopy with APEX2 labeling.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge the localization data, they note that 'validation of these models is incomplete' and express concern that 'it remains unclear whether the different mutations affect SLC6A17 expression levels, subcellular localization, or the expression and trafficking of other SV and synapse components.' The lack of direct functional validation limits confidence in the localization claims.

results.result: LC-MS analysis of immunoisolated synaptic vesicles revealed that glutamine (Gln) is enriched in SVs, while eight other amino acids previously reported as SLC6A17 substrates in cell culture were not significantly enriched.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raise fundamental concerns about the interpretation of LC-MS data, stating that 'detection of Gln, along with classical neurotransmitters such as glutamate, GABA, or ACh, in isolated SV fractions does not prove that Gln is transported into SVs by active transport.' They note that Gln 'appearance in SV samples can therefore also be explained by trapping in SVs during endocytosis, presence in other - contaminating - organelles, binding to membrane surfaces, and other processes.'

results.result: Viral overexpression of SLC6A17-HA in mouse brain dramatically increased Gln levels in synaptic vesicles, with Gln reaching approximately twice the level of GABA, while also moderately increasing Glu, GABA, and His.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note that 'direct assays of Gln uptake into SVs, which have the potential to stringently test key postulates of the authors, are lacking.' The overexpression data showing increased Gln is acknowledged but not sufficient without direct transport measurements to establish SLC6A17 as a Gln transporter.

results.result: Genetic knockout (germline Slc6a17-/-) and virally mediated knockout of Slc6a17 both resulted in selective reduction of Gln in synaptic vesicles, with no significant changes in classical neurotransmitters (Glu, GABA, ACh) or other amino acids.
results.evaluation: While the consistency across knockout models is noted, reviewers emphasize that 'the data interpretation provided by the authors lacks stringency with respect to the biophysics of plasma membrane and SV transporters.' The absence of direct transport assays means the reduction in Gln could reflect indirect effects rather than direct transport activity.

results.result: The human ID mutation P633R causes mislocalization of SLC6A17 outside synaptic vesicles, with the mutant protein remaining in the soma and not co-purifying with SV markers.
results.evaluation: Reviewers state that validation is incomplete and 'it remains unclear whether the different mutations affect SLC6A17 expression levels, subcellular localization, or the expression and trafficking of other SV and synapse components.' While the mislocalization data is presented, its interpretation requires more rigorous validation.

results.result: The human ID mutation G162R allows SLC6A17 to localize to synaptic vesicles but is defective in transporting Gln into SVs, as shown by overexpression experiments where Gln levels were much lower than with wild-type SLC6A17 overexpression.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note that 'direct measurements of the transport activity of SLC6A17 in the various genetic contexts studied' are missing. The inference that G162R is transport-defective is based on indirect LC-MS measurements rather than direct transport assays, which limits the robustness of this conclusion.

results.result: The P633R point mutation in endogenous Slc6a17 resulted in decreased Gln levels in synaptic vesicles without affecting classical neurotransmitters or other amino acids, correlating with the mislocalization phenotype and behavioral impairments.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note that 'corresponding molecular underpinnings, that is, the molecular role of SLC6A17 in synapses and the functional molecular consequences of disease-related SLC6A17 variations, remain unclear because corresponding informative experimental approaches are missing.' The correlation between mislocalization and Gln reduction is presented but mechanistic validation is lacking.

results.result: The authors conclude that SLC6A17 is necessary and sufficient for Gln transport into SVs, and that decreased SV Gln is the key pathogenetic mechanism in human intellectual disability caused by SLC6A17 mutations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that 'the main conceptual claims of the study appear insufficiently justified' and that 'corresponding molecular underpinnings...remain unclear because corresponding informative experimental approaches are missing – most importantly direct measurements of the transport activity of SLC6A17.' The strong mechanistic conclusions about necessity, sufficiency, and pathogenesis are not adequately supported by the evidence presented.

results.result: Slc6a17 expression was mapped across mouse brain regions, showing strong expression in dentate gyrus and CA3 hippocampus, basolateral amygdala, and other regions, with little expression in CA1 or CA2.
results.evaluation: These expression mapping claims are descriptive and not challenged by reviewers. They provide context for the behavioral studies and are treated as straightforward observational findings.

results.result: Slc6a17 knockout and P633R mutant mice showed no significant differences from wild-type in body weight, basal activity, or short-term memory tasks.
results.evaluation: These negative control findings are not questioned by reviewers and serve to establish the specificity of the cognitive deficits observed in other behavioral tests.

results.result: The P633R point mutation is classified as a loss-of-function (LOF) mutation based on phenotypic similarity to Slc6a17 knockout mice.
results.evaluation: This inference is accepted as reasonable given the similar behavioral phenotypes between P633R mutants and knockout mice, though reviewers note broader concerns about molecular validation.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on expression mapping claims C18-C21. Both evaluations find these descriptive anatomical localization findings well-supported and uncontroversial.

Both address P633R mislocalization and Gln reduction (C73-C77). OpenEval finds claims supported with strong correlation, though notes C77's causation is inferential. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, emphasizing lack of mechanistic validation and missing direct functional approaches.

Both address behavioral phenotypes. OpenEval finds C22-C29 well-supported by comprehensive behavioral data. Peer reviewers explicitly state behavioral evidence is 'convincing' for C25-C29 and related claims, showing strong agreement on behavioral findings.

Partial overlap on negative control behavioral findings (C22-C24). OpenEval includes these in broader supported behavioral assessment. Peer reviewers separately acknowledge these negative controls as valid, establishing specificity of cognitive deficits.

Both address P633R behavioral phenotypes (C33-C37). OpenEval finds data supported with appropriate statistics. Peer reviewers accept behavioral abnormalities as convincing, showing agreement on phenotypic characterization despite broader concerns about molecular validation.

Overlap on negative behavioral controls C30-C32. OpenEval includes in overall supported assessment of P633R phenotype. Peer reviewers separately validate these as establishing specificity of deficits.

Both address C38 (P633R as LOF mutation). OpenEval rates as supported but notes conclusion relies on phenotypic comparison rather than direct functional assessment. Peer reviewers accept this inference as reasonable given similar behavioral phenotypes.

Both address SV localization claims C39-C45. OpenEval finds strongly supported by convergent evidence from multiple orthogonal techniques. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, noting validation is incomplete and expressing concern about whether mutations affect expression levels or trafficking of other components.

Both address C46 (proteomics validation). OpenEval finds supported by TMT proteomics showing SLC6A17 as only reduced transporter. Peer reviewers include this in broader UNCERTAIN assessment of localization, noting incomplete validation despite acknowledging the data.

Both address P633R mislocalization (C47-C48). OpenEval finds supported by convergent imaging and biochemistry evidence. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, stating validation is incomplete and it remains unclear whether mutations affect localization or other components.

Both address Gln enrichment in immunoisolated SVs (C49-C51). OpenEval finds supported by LC-MS with appropriate controls, noting caveat about detectability. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, raising fundamental concern that detection doesn't prove active transport and could reflect trapping during endocytosis or contamination.

Both address C52-C53 (Gln in HA-tagged SV isolation). OpenEval finds this provides independent confirmation using different purification strategy. Peer reviewers include in UNCERTAIN rating, maintaining that detection doesn't prove transport mechanism.

Both address overexpression data C54-C58. OpenEval finds supported, demonstrating sufficiency with caveats about Glu/GABA increases. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, emphasizing that 'direct assays of Gln uptake into SVs...are lacking' and overexpression data insufficient without direct transport measurements.

Both address G162R mutant characterization (C59-C63). OpenEval finds supported with Syp-HA control distinguishing specific transport from general enrichment. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, explicitly noting 'direct measurements of transport activity...are missing' and inference is based on indirect LC-MS rather than transport assays.
Minimal overlap on C64 (G162R transport defect). OpenEval includes in supported assessment of G162R data. Peer reviewers include in UNCERTAIN rating emphasizing lack of direct transport assays.

Both address germline knockout LC-MS data (C65-C67). OpenEval finds supported as critical loss-of-function experiment establishing necessity. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, noting consistency but emphasizing 'data interpretation...lacks stringency' and absence of direct transport assays means reduction could reflect indirect effects.

Both address viral knockout data (C68-C72). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to inconsistent Glu/GABA increases versus germline knockout. Peer reviewers also rate UNCERTAIN, emphasizing lack of direct transport assays and questioning whether changes reflect direct transport activity.

Both address major mechanistic conclusions (C78, C80, C83-C84). OpenEval finds evidence strong with convergent data but notes causation claims remain inferential. Peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED, explicitly stating 'main conceptual claims...appear insufficiently justified' and 'corresponding informative experimental approaches are missing - most importantly direct measurements of transport activity.'

Minimal overlap on background claims C1, C10. OpenEval notes these are supported by literature citations establishing clinical relevance. Peer reviewers include these in broader acceptance of clinical context.
Minimal overlap on C13 (background literature). OpenEval finds background claims appropriately cited. Peer reviewers don't specifically evaluate but include C13 in localization assessment context.
OpenEval evaluates discussion claims C85-C88 as supported by citations and logical reasoning. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these interpretive discussion points.
